title: Concurrent Stream Limit
seoTitle: Design Netflix's Limit on Simultaneous Screens per Account
description: Design a system that limits how many screens an account can stream on at once — session leases, heartbeats, atomic counters and handling crashed devices.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.title: What is a Concurrent Stream Limit?
blocks.text: Streaming services limit how many devices can play video on one account at the same time — for example, a "Standard" plan allows 2 screens. Starting playback on a third device should be blocked until another stops.

items: When a device starts playback, allow it only if the account is under its plan's screen limit.
When playback stops, the screen should be freed.
If a device crashes or loses connectivity, its screen should be freed automatically.
Users should see which devices are currently streaming and be able to stop one.

blocks.question: What are the non-functional requirements for this system?

items: The limit must hold under concurrency — two devices starting at the same instant can't both take the last slot.
Checks add little latency to starting playback (< 100ms).
Highly available: if the limiter fails, prefer letting users watch over blocking paying customers.
Scale to 200M+ accounts and tens of millions of concurrent streams.

lines: - allow start if under plan limit
blocks.caption: Stream Limit Requirements

items: **Account**: plan and its maximum concurrent streams.
**Stream session (lease)**: accountId, deviceId, sessionId, last heartbeat, expiry.

blocks.code:
POST   /sessions { "deviceId": "tv-123", "titleId": "..." } -> { sessionId, ttl } | 409 LIMIT_REACHED
POST   /sessions/:id/heartbeat
DELETE /sessions/:id
GET    /accounts/:id/sessions -> Session[]

blocks.text: 1) Allow playback only under the limit

When a device starts playback, the player calls the **Session Service** before requesting the stream manifest. The service checks the account's active sessions and creates a new one only if there's room.
2) Free the screen when playback stops
On stop, the player deletes its session. The Playback API (manifest and DRM license requests) only works with a valid session ID, so a removed session also stops playback.

Sessions are **leases**: each has an expiry a minute or two in the future, and the player renews it with a heartbeat every 30 seconds. If a device dies, its heartbeats stop and the lease expires on its own — no cleanup message needed.
Listing sessions reads the account's active leases. "Stop streaming on this device" deletes the lease; the player's next heartbeat (or license renewal) fails and playback ends.
1) How do we enforce the limit correctly under concurrency?

approach.text: Count active sessions; if under the limit, insert a new one.

challenges.text: Two devices starting simultaneously both read "1 of 2" and both insert — three streams.

approach.text: Lock the account row (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`), count unexpired sessions, insert, commit.

challenges.text: Correct, but adds database latency to every heartbeat and start at tens of millions of streams.

approach.text: Keep each account's sessions in a Redis sorted set scored by expiry. A Lua script atomically (1) removes expired members (`ZREMRANGEBYSCORE`), (2) checks the count against the limit, and (3) adds the new session. Redis runs scripts single-threaded, so the check-and-add can't interleave. Heartbeats just update the member's score.

challenges.text: Redis must be replicated; a failover can briefly lose recent leases, which at worst lets an extra stream start — acceptable for this product.

blocks.text: 2) What if the session service is down?

**Fail open**: if the check times out, let playback start and attach a session later. Blocking millions of paying customers because a limiter is down is far worse than briefly allowing an extra screen. Monitor and alert on fail-open rates.

Short leases free crashed devices quickly but require frequent heartbeats; long leases reduce load but leave ghost sessions. A 30-second heartbeat with a 90-second lease (tolerating two missed heartbeats) is a common balance. Tie heartbeats to existing traffic — such as DRM license renewals — so they cost almost nothing extra.

quiz.question: Why model streams as leases with expiry?
options: So crashed devices free their slot automatically when heartbeats stop
quiz.explanation: Expiry removes the need for a reliable stop message.

quiz.question: What prevents two simultaneous starts from exceeding the limit?
options: An atomic check-and-add, e.g. a Redis Lua script
quiz.explanation: The count check and insert must happen as one atomic step.

quiz.question: If the session service is unavailable, what should happen?
quiz.explanation: Briefly allowing an extra stream beats blocking paying customers.

quiz.question: How can heartbeats be made nearly free?
options: Piggyback on existing DRM license renewals
quiz.explanation: Reusing traffic the player already sends avoids extra load.
